items.title: AMD acquires AI chip startup Taalas to boost inference performance by etching model weights into silicon [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: AMD acquires Taalas to boost inference performance by etching models in silicon
items.summary:
AMD has acquired Toronto-based AI chip startup Taalas, which develops model-specific integrated circuits that etch AI model weights directly into silicon to significantly accelerate inference performance. Taalas' first test chip demonstrated serving Meta's Llama 3.1 model at nearly 17,000 tokens per second, outperforming Nvidia GPUs and Cerebras accelerators by large margins.

The startup's approach involves embedding model weights in mask-ROM while using SRAM for caches and fine-tuning adapters, enabling efficient inference but limiting flexibility since any major model update requires chip respins. AMD plans to integrate Taalas' technology with its Instinct-based Helios racks, potentially offloading token generation to these specialized accelerators while handling prompt processing on GPUs, aiming to offer a high-performance AI platform for specific workloads.

items.summary:
OpenAI has improved GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT for Plus and Pro users to provide more reliable factual responses and more focused, adaptable answers. The update includes a new slider to control the depth of ChatGPT's reasoning. For free users, OpenAI has expanded access to GPT-5.6 Luna, enabling unlimited text chats and introducing a Think button that allows access to higher reasoning for more complex questions.

The improvements aim to support a wide range of user needs, from quick questions to complex planning and research. GPT-5.6 Sol now delivers clearer, more concise answers tailored to the question's complexity, avoiding unnecessary details and formatting. The update also enhances factual accuracy, especially for information involving dates, numbers, and rules. Free users benefit from expanded capabilities with GPT-5.6 Luna as the default model, improving accessibility to advanced AI features.

items.title: Study finds humans miss one in three AI agent command threats during 40,000 game runs simulating permission approvals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Humans missed 1 in 3 threats approving AI agent commands across 40k game runs
items.summary:
A browser game simulating human approval of AI agent commands revealed that players missed about one in three threats, with an average accuracy of 66.3% across over 40,000 runs and 409,000 approval decisions. The game tested users' ability to detect malicious commands under time pressure, highlighting challenges in human oversight of AI actions.

The study found that blatantly destructive commands were caught more reliably than those exfiltrating credentials, which were missed three times as often. A notable blind spot was the command "npm run analyze," approved 64.7% of the time despite containing hidden data exfiltration scripts, indicating users often overlook detailed command histories. The findings suggest that relying on users to approve AI commands may not be a strong safeguard, especially as approval fatigue increases with repeated prompts.

items.title: New Orleans deploys AI to answer 911 calls for triage and information, routing emergencies to human dispatchers to reduce call volume [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: New Orleans will use AI to answer 911 calls instead of a human
items.summary:
New Orleans' Orleans Parish Communication District has started using Carbyne's AI Emergency Call Triage system to answer 911 calls, aiming to manage high call volumes by automatically handling repeated or related calls and directing emergencies to human dispatchers. The AI was first implemented in April for 311 non-emergency calls and now assists with 911 calls by providing immediate feedback and routing callers appropriately.

The AI system is designed to reduce delays caused by multiple calls about the same incident, but officials emphasize that it does not replace human dispatchers for emergency calls. While the technology may improve response efficiency, concerns remain about potential biases in AI decision-making and challenges in accurately understanding diverse speech patterns, highlighting the need for human oversight and careful monitoring.

items.title: Researchers introduce the Ignition Index to quantify Global Workspace Theory dynamics in transformer language models across multiple architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Ignition Index: Measuring Global Workspace Dynamics in Language Models
items.summary: Researchers have developed the Ignition Index, a new metric that measures abrupt transitions in transformer language model layers, reflecting Global Workspace Theory's predictions. The metric distinguishes genuine linguistic processing from spurious effects and was tested across 11 models from five architecture families, showing feedforward transformers exhibit stronger ignition-like behavior than state-space models, while recurrent models show such transitions along their iteration dimension. The study also identified a phase transition during training in one model before the formation of specific attention mechanisms and found no correlation between ignition characteristics and model scale or input signal strength, suggesting a saturation effect in transformer architectures.

The study also identified a phase transition during training in one model before the formation of specific attention mechanisms and found no correlation between ignition characteristics and model scale or input signal strength, suggesting a saturation effect in transformer architectures.
items.originalSummary: Researchers have introduced the Ignition Index, a new metric designed to quantify the dynamics predicted by Global Workspace Theory within transformer language models. This metric measures the abruptness of transitions in model layer responses to input signals, distinguishing genuine linguistic processing from spurious effects. Analysis across multiple model architectures revealed that feedforward transformers exhibit more pronounced ignition-like behavior compared to state-space models, and recurrent architectures show such transitions along their iteration dimension. Additionally, a phase transition was detected during training in one model prior to the emergence of specific attention mechanisms. Contrary to some hypotheses, ignition characteristics did not correlate with model scale or input signal strength, suggesting a saturation effect in transformer architectures. The Ignition Index offers a validated quantitative tool linking cognitive theory with mechanistic interpretability in language models.

items.title: Researchers introduce EcoAgent-Bench to evaluate economic decision-making in budget-constrained LLM agents across 304 tasks with priced actions and explicit budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EcoAgent-Bench: Evaluating Economic Decision-Making in Budget-Constrained LLM Agents
items.summary:
EcoAgent-Bench is a new benchmark designed to assess how large language model (LLM) agents make economic decisions under budget constraints, focusing on task completion with priced actions and explicit budgets. The benchmark includes 304 tasks derived from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, testing decisions such as when to escalate, model tier selection, and stopping on unsupported premises. Seven LLM agents and four oracle controls were evaluated in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, revealing that agents often either escalate unnecessarily or fail to escalate when needed, resulting in low economic consistency scores.

The study found that micro-averaged accuracy can reward one-sided policies like always escalating, which perform poorly on save-oriented tasks, prompting the introduction of an economic-consistency score to better capture balanced performance. Tool-API agents achieved only 3.9% to 24.0% strict success rates and up to 7.3% economic consistency, with GPT-5.4's escalation rate increasing marginally from 0% to 3% under budget changes. The results highlight that task completion under budget and economical action selection are distinct challenges. The researchers have released the task bundle, transformation pipeline, evaluation environments, and result artifacts to support further study.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent benchmarks usually measure task completion and treat resource use as an auxiliary statistic. In deployment, however, the choice among a local lookup, broad search, composite research tool, stronger model, or human escalation is part of the task itself. We introduce EcoAgent-Bench, in which every task specifies priced actions and an explicit budget. Its 304 real-derived tasks span five families adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, and test four decisions: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting a model tier, and stopping on unsupported premises. We evaluate seven LLM agents in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, together with four oracle scripted controls. Micro-averaged accuracy rewards one-sided policies: always-escalate controls achieve high micro success while failing save-oriented tasks. We therefore also report an economic-consistency score (the worse of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups) which exposes this failure. Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% micro strict success (at most 7.3% economic consistency), often either stopping before warranted escalation or overspending on cheap tasks. A threshold-crossing budget sweep changes GPT-5.4's escalation rate from 0% to only 3%. These results show that completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct properties. We release the task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and integrity-bound result artifacts needed to study both.

items.title: Research proposes a multi-layered, compliance-first AI architecture for hospitals integrating agent orchestration, policy centralization, and privacy-preserving data fabric [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: From Siloed Algorithms to Compliance-First Agentic Platforms: A Multi-Layered Architecture for Hospital AI Systems
items.summary:
Hospitals increasingly use AI for tasks like triage and scheduling, but most systems remain isolated within departments, causing duplicated efforts and governance challenges. This research introduces a hospital-specific AI platform architecture featuring an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows, a Compliance and Policy Layer centralizing regulations such as HIPAA and GDPR, and a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric incorporating federated learning and differential privacy.

Using a synthetic hospital dataset and an open prototype, the study demonstrates coordinated triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, resulting in simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation while maintaining secure data access. The architecture offers a practical blueprint for hospital leaders to transition from fragmented AI tools to governed, globally compliant platforms adaptable to on-premise, hybrid, or cloud deployments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.06112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.

items.title: Researchers introduce HarnessOpt-Bench to evaluate LLMs on automated harness optimization across multiple tasks and models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark designed to measure how well large language models (LLMs) perform automated harness optimization, which involves iteratively improving the prompts, tools, and orchestration code surrounding an AI system. The benchmark evaluates LLMs as optimizers by providing them with a seed harness, graded feedback, and a fixed evaluation budget to edit and improve the harness, with performance measured by normalized gains on held-out test data.

The study tested five leading LLMs across four downstream tasks using both a shared coding harness and their native harnesses over 111 runs. Results showed that optimizer models had a greater impact than the coding harnesses they used, native harnesses were not consistently better, and performance gains varied significantly depending on the task and initial conditions. These findings establish harness optimization as a measurable capability with substantial room for improvement in AI systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.06301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed within agentic systems, their capabilities depend not only on the model weights but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration code surrounding them. This makes automated harness optimization -- the iterative and evaluation-guided improvement of a harness by an AI system -- both an important route to improving AI systems and a demanding capability for AI systems themselves. Yet the community lacks a common protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform at this task. We introduce HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization under expensive and stochastic evaluation. An optimizer, an LLM paired with a coding harness, receives a target agent's seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget. It edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, which is scored by its normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition that remains inaccessible throughout search. A trusted execution environment enforces the evaluation boundary, meters target-agent resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit. We evaluate 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers both under a shared coding harness and under their native harnesses across 4 downstream tasks, over 111 scored runs. Experiment results show that optimizer models separate more than the coding harnesses they act through, native harnesses are not consistently superior, and gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes. These results establish harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with large space for improvement.

items.title: Study finds PCA-based dimensionality reduction improves Persian speech emotion recognition using Whisper, with limited gains from ASR fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Study of ASR Adaptation and Representation Dimensionality Reduction in Persian Speech Emotion Recognition Using Whisper
items.summary:
Researchers investigated the use of Whisper, a large pretrained speech model, for Persian speech emotion recognition (SER), focusing on reducing representation dimensionality and adapting the model to the Persian language. They proposed a framework that applies principal component analysis (PCA) to frame-level embeddings from Whisper, reducing trainable parameters and improving performance on the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent protocol. Fine-tuning Whisper on a Persian automatic speech recognition (ASR) task provided only modest improvements for SER, indicating limited transfer from ASR adaptation to emotion recognition in this context.

The PCA-based approach also reduced training latency and memory usage by eliminating the need for learned projection layers, while an attention-based pooling mechanism aggregated the reduced embeddings for classification with a lightweight prediction head. These findings offer practical insights for efficiently applying large pretrained speech models to emotion recognition tasks in low-resource languages like Persian.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) in low-resource languages remains a challenging problem due to limited labeled data. In this work, we study the use of Whisper for Persian SER with a particular focus on representation dimensionality reduction and language-specific model adaptation. We propose a SER framework in which frame-level embeddings extracted from the Whisper encoder are reduced in dimensionality using PCA, eliminating the need for learned projection layers and substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters. The reduced representations are aggregated using an attention-based pooling mechanism and classified with a lightweight prediction head. In addition, we investigate whether fine-tuning Whisper on a Persian automatic speech recognition (ASR) task improves downstream SER performance. Experiments conducted on the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent evaluation protocol show that PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves emotion recognition performance while reducing training latency and memory usage. ASR fine-tuning yields only modest gains for SER, suggesting limited transfer from language adaptation to emotion-related representations under the evaluated conditions. These findings provide practical insights into the efficient use of large pretrained speech models for emotion recognition in low-resource languages.

items.title: Researchers propose GROM, a gradient-free one-shot machine unlearning method that rapidly removes targeted knowledge from large language models with a closed-form solution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning
items.summary:
Researchers introduce GROM, a novel machine unlearning technique that eliminates specific sensitive knowledge from large language models without iterative fine-tuning. Unlike traditional gradient-based methods, GROM uses a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization to compute a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices, applying the change in seconds through gradient-free forward passes.

GROM preserves model behavior on retained data while suppressing unwanted content, achieving state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on benchmarks such as TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News, and WMDP. The method also resists low-bit quantization attacks that can recover erased content in gradient-based approaches. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further use and evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine unlearning has become a critical capability for safely removing specific, sensitive knowledge from large language models (LLMs). Current state-of-the-art approaches primarily rely on iterative, training-time unlearning via fine-tuning. However, even when utilizing parameter-efficient dimensionality reduction techniques like LoRA, gradient-based optimization remains computationally expensive and lacks explicit analytical formulations. It can also leave the targeted knowledge merely hidden rather than removed, to the point that simply quantizing the unlearned model restores much of what it was supposed to have erased. To resolve this, we propose a novel one-shot unlearning approach, abandoning iterative optimization in favor of a direct, exact analytical solution. We frame the unlearning process as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices. This update forces the selected layer to suppress unwanted content while strictly preserving its behavior on retained data. Computed from gradient-free forward passes alone, with no backpropagation and no iteration to convergence, GROM applies the weight edit in mere seconds, which makes it orders of magnitude faster than traditional fine-tuning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing overall model performance. Because the update removes the targeted content from the weights instead of masking it, GROM also withstands the low-bit quantization attack that recovers much of the content a gradient-based baseline had appeared to forget. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/GROM.

items.title: Researchers introduce AV-AIVAT for 74x cheaper agent evaluation with certified anytime-valid stopping in imperfect-information games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AV-AIVAT: 74x Cheaper Agent Evaluation with Certified Anytime-Valid Stopping in Imperfect-Information Games
items.summary: Researchers present AV-AIVAT, a method combining the Action-Informed Value Assessment Tool (AIVAT) with continuously monitored Confidence Sequences (CSs) to enable efficient, auditable early stopping in agent evaluations for imperfect-information games. This approach reduces variance and allows evaluations to stop as soon as sufficient evidence is gathered, maintaining statistical guarantees. AV-AIVAT was tested across 15 large language model agent configurations in Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, showing a median 74-fold reduction in the number of hands needed to reach a decision compared to raw outcomes under asymptotic confidence sequences. The method also includes exact finite-sample certification using Empirical-Bernstein CS, demonstrated structurally for Leduc hold'em, and provides tools for third-party verification of evaluation results at stopping time.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.06362v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deciding which of two agents is stronger means playing games until skill outweighs luck, and every game costs money, model inference, or expert time. Since the number of games needed is unknown, fixed-budget evaluations either keep paying after the result is settled or stop before the agents can be told apart, while naive optional stopping with an ordinary confidence interval invalidates the stated level. We make such an evaluation stop as soon as its evidence suffices, with the guarantee intact. The Action-Informed Value Assessment Tool (AIVAT) reduces variance in imperfect-information games through conditional mean-zero corrections, by a median $54\times$ across 15 LLM agent configurations spanning 71,439 paired Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em (HUNL) hands, but does not say when to stop. We combine AIVAT with continuously monitored Confidence Sequences (CSs) into anytime-valid AIVAT (AV-AIVAT), whose online value model learns only from past games so that no game scores its own correction. At the nominal 95\% level and a target precision of $\pm1$ Big Blind, raw outcomes need a median $74\times$ as many hands as AIVAT-corrected outcomes to stop under the Asymptotic CS (AsympCS). Exact finite-sample certification uses the Empirical-Bernstein CS (EB-CS), which needs an independently justified bound on corrected payoffs. We establish such a bound structurally for Leduc hold'em and characterize a width floor set by the CS's bet cap and that bound, which governs how much of a variance gain becomes earlier stopping; the descriptive HUNL EB-CS runs show a median $1.37\times$ stopping-time ratio. AV-AIVAT turns variance reduction into efficient, auditable early stopping while separating asymptotic screening from exact certification, so an evaluation can stop the moment its evidence suffices and hand a third party everything needed to recheck the verdict at that very stopping time.

items.title: Researchers introduce SCOPE to improve language model selective trust by reducing errors from misleading context while preserving accuracy on valid context [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning When to Trust via Selective Context Preference Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers address the challenge of language models being misled by external signals that can flip correct answers to wrong ones. They introduce MIST, a human-annotated benchmark with four context conditions, and SC2W, a metric measuring susceptibility to misleading signals. Their study finds this vulnerability is widespread across models.

To mitigate this, they propose SCOPE, which optimizes model training using balanced preference pairs across all context types rather than focusing only on misleading cases. This approach significantly reduces errors caused by misleading context in popular open-source models while maintaining accuracy when context is clean, correct, or irrelevant. The work emphasizes evaluating models based on selective trust rather than mere resistance to misleading information.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.06377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models increasingly condition their answers on external signals, and a single misleading one can turn a correct answer wrong. The obvious remedy, training models to resist such signals, hides a failure mode: a model that ignores all context looks robust yet is useless when the context is worth trusting. We recast the problem as selective trust and introduce MIST, a human-annotated benchmark that renders each reasoning item under four matched conditions (clean, misleading, correct-context, and irrelevant-context), together with SC2W, a paired metric counting how often a misleading signal flips a clean-correct answer to wrong. Across a comprehensive benchmark study, we observe that such a susceptibility is universal. We then propose SCOPE, which mines clean-correct/misleading-wrong failures and optimizes a standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective over matched preference pairs balanced equally across all four conditions, rather than over misleading items alone. Our approach substantially reduces SC2W on popular open-sourced models while preserving accuracy when the added context is clean, correct, or irrelevant. With this work, we argue that models should be judged on selective trust, not on resistance alone.

items.title: Researchers find test-time scaling in reasoning models often fails to improve accuracy and increases hallucinations on knowledge-intensive tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models Is Not Effective for Knowledge-Intensive Tasks Yet
items.summary: A study evaluating 14 reasoning models shows that increasing inference-time computation through longer reasoning chains does not consistently enhance accuracy in closed-book knowledge-intensive tasks and often leads to more factuality hallucinations. The research identifies that longer reasoning encourages more attempts to answer, many incorrect, and reveals confirmation bias where extended reasoning reinforces early errors with fabricated details. The authors also provide an information-theoretic explanation that compute-only test-time scaling cannot introduce new information about the correct answer, highlighting limitations of current methods for these tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2509.06861v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Test-time scaling increases inference-time computation through longer reasoning chains and has shown strong performance gains across many domains. However, frontier models still suffer from factuality hallucinations, raising the question of whether increased computation is effective on closed-book knowledge-intensive tasks. In this work, we evaluate 14 reasoning models under different test-time scaling strategies. Our results challenge its effectiveness: increasing test-time computation does not consistently improve accuracy and often leads to more hallucinations. We find that changes in hallucination rates are largely driven by the model's willingness to answer, as longer reasoning encourages more attempts, many of which are incorrect. We also observe patterns consistent with confirmation bias, where extended reasoning reinforces early incorrect beliefs with fabricated details. Finally, we provide an information-theoretic perspective showing that compute-only test-time scaling, as a post-processing procedure of a fixed model, cannot introduce new information about the ground-truth answer, explaining the limited performance gains. Overall, our findings highlight important limitations of current test-time scaling methods for closed-book knowledge-intensive tasks. Code and data are available at https://github.com/XuZhao0/tts-knowledge

items.title: CRINN uses reinforcement learning to optimize approximate nearest neighbor search algorithms, achieving top performance on multiple benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CRINN: Contrastive Reinforcement Learning for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
items.summary:
CRINN introduces a new approach to approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) by framing optimization as a reinforcement learning problem that rewards execution speed while maintaining accuracy. The method automatically generates faster ANNS implementations and demonstrates superior or tied top performance on five out of six widely-used benchmark datasets compared to state-of-the-art open-source algorithms.

The research highlights CRINN's potential beyond ANNS optimization by showing that large language models augmented with reinforcement learning can automate complex algorithmic improvements that typically require specialized expertise and manual effort. The code for CRINN is publicly available for further exploration and use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2508.02091v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) algorithms have become increasingly critical for recent AI applications, particularly in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agent-based LLM applications. In this paper, we present CRINN, a new paradigm for ANNS algorithms. CRINN treats ANNS optimization as a reinforcement learning problem where execution speed serves as the reward signal. This approach enables the automatic generation of progressively faster ANNS implementations while maintaining accuracy constraints. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates CRINN's effectiveness across six widely-used NNS benchmark datasets. When compared against state-of-the-art open-source ANNS algorithms, CRINN achieves best performance on three of them (GIST-960-Euclidean, MNIST-784-Euclidean, and GloVe-25-angular), and tied for first place on two of them (SIFT-128-Euclidean and GloVe-25-angular). The implications of CRINN's success reach well beyond ANNS optimization: It validates that LLMs augmented with reinforcement learning can function as an effective tool for automating sophisticated algorithmic optimizations that demand specialized knowledge and labor-intensive manual refinement. Code can be found at https://github.com/ornith-ai/CRINN

items.title: Researchers propose All-Quadrant Bounded Clipping GRPO to fix unbounded updates in reinforcement learning with large language models, improving stability and generalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: All-Quadrant Bounded Clipping GRPO: Closing the Unbounded Blind Spot for Stable and Generalizable Training
items.summary:
Researchers identify a structural blind spot in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) used for reinforcement learning with large language models, where negative advantage combined with increased likelihood ratio leads to unbounded suppressive updates that reduce entropy and reasoning capacity. To address this, they introduce All-Quadrant Bounded Clipping GRPO (ABC-GRPO), which applies clipping across all four quadrants of the likelihood-ratio and advantage space to ensure bounded policy updates.

ABC-GRPO clips the likelihood ratio before multiplying by the advantage, adding a trust-region floor and cap in specific quadrants to maintain stable policy displacement. Evaluations on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 base models show ABC-GRPO outperforms GRPO, SAPO, and dual-clip PPO, and is competitive with the strongest baseline DAPO, while preserving higher entropy. The improvements also transfer to other benchmarks including MATH-500 and out-of-domain code generation (HumanEval). Ablation studies confirm the dominant role of the previously unbounded quadrant in limiting performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.03895v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has emerged as a popular algorithm for reinforcement learning with large language models (LLMs). However, GRPO inherits PPO's token-level clipping while replacing token-level advantages with a single sequence-level advantage. Through a four-quadrant analysis of the (likelihood-ratio, advantage) space, we show that this combination leaves one quadrant -- negative advantage combined with an increased likelihood ratio (Q4) -- structurally unbounded, so that a few high-ratio tokens can receive very large suppressive updates that collapse entropy and narrow the reasoning boundary. To address this, we propose All-Quadrant Bounded Clipping GRPO (ABC-GRPO), which applies unconditional clipping in all four quadrants through sign-dependent boundaries. ABC-GRPO clips the likelihood ratio before multiplying by the advantage, adding a trust-region floor in Q2 and a cap in Q4 -- its negative-advantage branch coinciding with dual-clip PPO -- to yield bounded per-step policy displacement in every quadrant. On mathematical reasoning with Qwen3 base models, ABC-GRPO attains the highest Avg@64 and Pass@64: it is statistically superior to GRPO, SAPO, and dual-clip PPO and competitive with the strongest baseline (DAPO), while maintaining substantially higher entropy; the gains transfer to MATH-500 and to out-of-domain code (HumanEval). Ablations isolate Q4 as the dominant blind spot.

items.title: Researchers present Online Reasoning Calibration (ORCA) to improve large language model reasoning efficiency and generalization through test-time training and conformal prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Online Reasoning Calibration: Test-Time Training Enables Generalizable Conformal LLM Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers introduce Online Reasoning Calibration (ORCA), a framework that calibrates the sampling process of large language models using conformal prediction and test-time training to provide valid confidence estimates under distributional shifts. ORCA employs a meta-learning procedure that updates the calibration module for each input, addressing inefficiencies caused by miscalibration in post-trained models and sampling techniques. The method offers theoretical guarantees on conformal risks and demonstrates improved efficiency and generalization across various reasoning tasks. Empirical results show that ORCA can reduce compute costs by up to 47.5% on in-distribution tasks and significantly improve savings in zero-shot out-of-domain settings while maintaining low error rates. The code for ORCA is publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.01170v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While test-time scaling has enabled large language models to solve highly difficult tasks, state-of-the-art results come at exorbitant compute costs. These inefficiencies can be attributed to the miscalibration of post-trained language models, and the lack of calibration in popular sampling techniques. Here, we present Online Reasoning Calibration (ORCA), a framework for calibrating the sampling process that draws upon conformal prediction and test-time training. Specifically, we introduce a meta-learning procedure that updates the calibration module for each input. This allows us to provide valid confidence estimates under distributional shift, e.g. in thought patterns that occur across different stages of reasoning, or in prompt distributions between model development and deployment. ORCA not only provides theoretical guarantees on conformal risks, but also empirically shows higher efficiency and generalization across different reasoning tasks. At risk level $\delta=0.1$, ORCA improves Qwen2.5-32B efficiency on in-distribution tasks with savings up to 47.5% with supervised labels and 40.7% with self-consistency labels. Under zero-shot out-of-domain settings, it improves MATH-500 savings from 24.8% of the static calibration baseline to 67.0% while maintaining a low empirical error rate, and the same trend holds across model families and downstream benchmarks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzekai99/ORCA.

items.title: Researchers prove a fundamental trade-off in long-sequence models limiting simultaneous efficiency, compactness, and recall capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Impossibility Triangle of Long-Context Modeling
items.summary:
Researchers identify and prove a fundamental trade-off in long-sequence models, showing that no model can simultaneously achieve per-step computation independent of sequence length (efficiency), state size independent of sequence length (compactness), and recall proportional to sequence length (recall). They formalize this within an Online Sequence Processor framework that includes Transformers, state space models, and recurrent networks. Using information-theoretic inequalities, they prove that models satisfying efficiency and compactness have limited recall capacity dependent on model dimension and vocabulary size.

The study classifies 52 architectures published before March 2026 according to this trade-off, demonstrating that each achieves at most two of the three properties, with hybrid models tracing continuous trajectories within the trade-off space. Experiments on synthetic associative recall tasks with five representative architectures validate the theoretical bound, confirming that empirical recall capacity remains below the information-theoretic limit and no architecture escapes the trade-off triangle.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.05066v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We identify and prove a fundamental trade-off governing long-sequence models: no model can simultaneously achieve (i) per-step computation independent of sequence length (Efficiency), (ii) state size independent of sequence length (Compactness), and (iii) the ability to recall a number of historical facts proportional to sequence length (Recall). We formalize this trade-off within an Online Sequence Processor abstraction that unifies Transformers, state space models, linear recurrent networks, and their hybrids. Using the Data Processing Inequality and Fano's Inequality, we prove that any model satisfying Efficiency and Compactness can recall at most O(poly(d)/log V) key-value pairs from a sequence of arbitrary length, where d is the model dimension and V is the vocabulary size. We classify 52 architectures published before March 2026 into the triangle, showing that each achieves at most two of the three properties and that hybrid architectures trace continuous trajectories in the interior. Experiments on synthetic associative recall tasks with five representative architectures validate the theoretical bound: empirical recall capacity lies strictly below the information-theoretic limit, and no architecture escapes the triangle.

items.title: Researchers propose stage-wise preference optimization to reduce hallucination in vision-language models by targeting multimodal data near failure boundaries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reducing Hallucination in Vision-Language Models via Stage-wise Preference Optimization under Distribution Shift
items.summary:
Researchers propose a stage-wise preference optimization framework to reduce hallucination in vision-language models (VLMs), addressing the issue where models generate linguistically plausible but visually inconsistent responses. Their approach constructs hallucination-focused preference pairs emphasizing ambiguous spatial orientation, object relationships, OCR uncertainty, and adversarial false-premise training to improve grounding consistency and reduce hallucination.

Experiments on open-source benchmarks and real-world multimodal evaluations show that this method produces more visually grounded responses than several leading proprietary VLMs, particularly in challenging scenarios involving ambiguous spatial reasoning and adversarial inputs. The findings suggest hallucination arises not only from limited model capacity but also from autoregressive generation favoring plausible continuations under weak visual grounding, pointing to future research directions in physical consistency modeling and uncertainty-aware multimodal reasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.16411v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hallucination remains a fundamental challenge in vision-language models (VLMs), where autoregressive generation may produce linguistically plausible yet physically inconsistent or visually ungrounded responses due to likelihood maximization under joint probabilistic modeling. We propose a stage-wise preference optimization framework for hallucination reduction through targeted multimodal data construction. Rather than directly optimizing on generic instruction-following data, our approach progressively constructs hallucination-focused preference pairs near known failure boundaries. The framework emphasizes ambiguous spatial orientation, object relationships, OCR uncertainty, and adversarial false-premise training. Hallucinated negatives are generated through minimally perturbed yet visually inconsistent alternatives, enabling Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to better separate grounded reasoning from plausible hallucination. Experiments on open-source benchmarks and real-world multimodal evaluation scenarios demonstrate improved grounding consistency, reduced hallucination, and more informative grounded responses. Cross-model qualitative evaluation further shows that the proposed multimodal LLM DPO framework produces more visually grounded responses than several frontier proprietary VLMs, such as in ambiguous spatial reasoning and adversarial false-premise settings. The results suggest that hallucination may arise not only from limited model capacity, but also from inherent tendencies of autoregressive probabilistic generation to favor linguistically plausible continuations under weak visual grounding. Future work may explore physical consistency modeling, uncertainty-aware multimodal reasoning, and architectural alternatives beyond standard autoregressive decoding.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.20247v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a major obstacle to continual learning in large language models (LLMs) and vision--language models (VLMs). Although Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer an efficient path to scaling, existing LoRA-based MoE continual learning methods still face a fundamental trade-off: they either isolate experts too aggressively, limiting knowledge transfer across tasks, or allow task-specific updates to overwrite important existing parameters, leading to severe forgetting. To address this, we propose CP-MoE, a continual learning framework built around a transient expert that captures early task-specific updates and guides their integration into stable experts. CP-MoE introduces a consistency-preserving routing bias, which uses the transient expert to estimate representation similarity with stable experts and steer routing towards more compatible expert selection, and a transient expert-guided regularisation mechanism, which selectively protects important historical parameters during merging. Together, these components reduce parameter interference and forgetting while preserving cross-task knowledge transfer. We validate CP-MoE on both unimodal and multimodal continual learning benchmarks with LLM-based and VLM-based MoE models. On SuperNI benchmark, spanning diverse sequential language tasks, CP-MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance and stronger zero-shot transfer to unseen tasks. On VQA v2 dataset, it scales effectively to multimodal visual reasoning, consistently reduces forgetting, and outperforms strong MoE baselines.

items.title: EuroExec benchmark shows frontier language models solve only 56.9% of European executive tasks compared to near-ceiling expert performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EuroExec: Frontier Language Models Fall Short of Expert Judgment on European Executive Decision Tasks
items.summary: Researchers evaluated six leading large language models (LLMs) on EuroExec, a benchmark of 413 open-ended European executive decision tasks created by 47 domain experts. Each model response was manually assessed using a detailed rubric and preference rankings, revealing the best model solved just 56.9% of tasks while expert answers were preferred in 74% of comparisons. The study highlights that current frontier LLMs fall significantly short of professional expert standards on complex, real-world decision problems and that human evaluation remains essential for accurate assessment.

The study highlights that current frontier LLMs fall significantly short of professional expert standards on complex, real-world decision problems and that human evaluation remains essential for accurate assessment.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04549v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frontier LLMs are increasingly put to use on open-ended complex questions, different in nature from the ones they are typically evaluated on. We dedicate more than 4,000 human expert hours to evaluate a selection of six frontier LLMs on a member of this class of problems: EuroExec, our introduced human expert-based benchmark composed of 413 open-ended long-form European executive tasks authored by 47 vetted domain experts, each question drawn from experience in a real case. Every response is manually evaluated through a multi-attribute rubric, an item-specific checklist of requirements, and a preference rank ordering, extracting an aggregate metric "Solve Rate". The strongest model solves only 56.9% of tasks, while expert-written reference answers judged blindly are solved at near-ceiling levels and are preferred over every model response in 74% of direct rankings, placing frontier generative systems well below the professional standard of work they are already used for. We see that the best way to extract this kind of conclusion is by employing human evaluators, carefully checking their consistency through rigorous statistical analysis, and observe that automatic measurements also fall short when evaluating on this case of real-world open-ended problems with a subjective ground truth.

items.title: Researchers propose A-SR, a self-evolving agentic LLM framework for symbolic regression that improves formula discovery accuracy across scientific domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A-SR: Self-Evolving Agentic LLMs for Symbolic Regression via Hierarchical Coordination
items.summary:
Researchers have developed A-SR, a self-evolving agentic framework for symbolic regression that coordinates formula discovery through hierarchical coordination protocols and role-conditioned evidence views. The framework adapts search processes within runs without updating LLM parameters and distills recorded trajectories into open-source LLMs across runs, improving accuracy significantly over baselines on benchmark scientific domains.

A-SR routes evaluator feedback to update role-level utilities and manage elite motifs, failure traces, and diagnostics among agents. Tested on four real-world scientific discovery tasks, A-SR achieved the best normalized mean squared error on seven of eight metrics, demonstrating improved reliability and productivity in symbolic regression compared to existing LLM-guided methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.04872v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Symbolic regression aims to discover closed-form equations from data, but existing LLM-guided methods often rely on a unified proposal loop that compresses heterogeneous search failures into a scalar score and a single prompt. We propose A-SR, a self-evolving agentic framework that shifts the control unit from expression edits to role-conditioned evidence views. A-SR coordinates formula discovery through routing among coordination protocols, an online evaluator-reward role policy, and state-routed process memory. During search, evaluator feedback characterizes reliability and productivity, updates role-level utilities, and routes elite motifs, failure traces, and validity diagnostics to different agents. The framework self-evolves at two timescales: within a run, it adapts the search process without updating LLM parameters; across runs, recorded trajectories can be distilled into open-source LLMs as role-conditioned proposal priors. Averaged over the four LSR-Synth scientific domains in LLM-SRBench, A-SR improves Acc@0.01 over baselines from 25.79% to 48.30% with Llama3.1-8B, while A-SR-LoRA improves the corresponding Qwen3-4B result from 24.58% to 38.29%. On four real-world scientific discovery tasks, A-SR obtains the best in-distribution or out-of-distribution normalized mean squared error on 7 of 8 reported metrics.

items.originalTitle: Agentic Nesting: A New Methodology for Existing Enterprise Application Integration and Services
items.summary: A new methodology called Agentic Nesting has been proposed to improve enterprise application integration by encapsulating existing applications as autonomous AI agents organized in a hierarchical structure. This approach aims to reduce architectural coupling and operational costs while enabling natural-language interaction and autonomous operation across heterogeneous systems. The framework includes a central orchestrator for coordinating tasks among agents and offers a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process management. The methodology introduces the concepts of "Application-as-Agent" and "Conversation-as-Integration," targeting enhanced intelligence capabilities and scalable coordination in complex enterprise ecosystems.

items.title: Researchers propose Woodpecker Distillation to improve strong language models by using weak models to identify and correct localized reasoning errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Woodpecker Distillation: Weak Models Diagnose Reasoning Bugs in Strong Models
items.summary: Researchers have developed Woodpecker Distillation, a training framework that enhances the reasoning performance of large language models by leveraging weak models to diagnose and correct localized reasoning bugs in stronger models. This method contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model interventions to create a corrective teacher distribution, which is then distilled into the strong model to guide its future reasoning steps toward correct solutions. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks demonstrate that this approach consistently improves strong-model accuracy and outperforms direct fine-tuning on corrected outputs.

items.originalSummary: Researchers have introduced Woodpecker Distillation, a training framework designed to improve the reasoning abilities of large language models. The approach identifies and corrects localized reasoning errors in strong models by leveraging interventions from weaker models, which guide the reasoning process toward correct solutions. Unlike direct fine-tuning on corrected outputs, this method distills corrective signals based on contrasting successful and unsuccessful reasoning paths, leading to enhanced performance on mathematical reasoning tasks.

items.originalTitle: From Continuous Predictors to Clinical Thresholds: Early Evidence on Performance Trade-offs of Guideline-Based Categorisation for Ischaemic Stroke Outcome Prediction
items.summary: A recent study evaluated whether continuous predictors in machine learning models for 90-day acute ischaemic stroke outcome prediction can be replaced by categorical encodings aligned with clinical guidelines without losing accuracy. Using data from a multi-centre European registry divided into three treatment cohorts, researchers compared standard gradient-boosted models with versions using guideline-based categorical thresholds. The categorised models performed comparably to continuous models in two cohorts but showed a significant accuracy decline in one cohort. Feature importance rankings remained consistent across models, indicating that guideline-based categorisation preserves key prognostic factors. This suggests that adopting clinical guideline-aligned categories is a feasible approach for stroke outcome prediction models.

items.originalTitle: SkillTrace: Multi-Trace Provenance Auditing for LLM-Agent Skill Reuse
items.summary: SkillTrace is a framework designed to audit the reuse of skills in large language model (LLM) agent ecosystems by extracting and comparing three types of provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structures, with an LLM assisting in extracting this trace during ingestion. Evaluations on the SKILLTRACE-BENCH dataset show high accuracy, and a large-scale audit demonstrates that trace-attributed evidence can improve skill reuse review beyond traditional repository-level methods.

items.originalSummary: The paper introduces SKILLTRACE, a framework designed to audit the reuse of skills within large language model (LLM) agent ecosystems. Unlike traditional code clone detection methods that focus on single-modality source code or entire package similarity, SKILLTRACE analyzes multiple traces of provenance—Expression, Implementation, and Operational—to detect skill reuse more comprehensively. The Operational Trace is represented as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG), capturing activation, procedure, and resource-flow structures. An LLM assists in extracting the Operational Trace during ingestion, while audits compare cached traces deterministically and calibrate them against strict negatives to support reuse decisions. items.title: Otter AI predicts human chess moves using time-aware, history-conditioned model with 15.3M parameters, surpassing Maia 2 on 117M Lichess rapid games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Otter: A Time-Aware, History-Conditioned Human Chess AI
items.summary:
Otter is a human chess AI that predicts moves by considering the last 20 moves and clock pressure, treating chess as a sequential, time-aware process rather than isolated positions. It was trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million rapid games on Lichess and achieves 55.23% top-1 move prediction accuracy, outperforming previous models like Maia 2 despite using fewer parameters and less data.

The model's accuracy varies across player skill levels, peaking at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 Elo bracket. Otter's code, trained models, and training logs have been publicly released, demonstrating that incorporating move history and time control improves human move prediction in chess AI.

items.originalTitle: Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks
items.summary: Researchers created a benchmarking and trace-logging framework to evaluate how different agent architectures impact performance in controlling microscopy tasks using large language model agents. They tested 105 agent configurations across 53 microscopy tasks with nearly 2,000 runs, comparing factors like agent number, LLM type, and retrieval-augmented generation parameters. The benchmarks effectively support qualification, regression testing, and direct comparison of agent configurations but do not reliably predict performance on new, unseen microscopy tasks, indicating limitations in generalizing agentic control systems beyond tested scenarios.

items.title: Researchers propose SCP-NL2TL, a selective conformal prediction framework that verifies reliability of natural language to temporal logic translations for safer autonomous system specifications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SCP-NL2TL: Selective Conformal Prediction with Semantic Verification for Natural Language to Temporal Logic Specifications
items.summary: Researchers introduce SCP-NL2TL, a framework that translates natural language instructions into formal temporal logic specifications while assessing their reliability to prevent unsafe or incorrect interpretations in autonomous systems. The method uses two black-box signals—back-translation fidelity and translation dispersion—to score reliability and applies conformal risk control to decide whether to accept or abstain from a specification, with an anomaly detector screening out-of-distribution inputs before translation. Experiments on Signal Temporal Logic, Linear Temporal Logic, and Spatio-Temporal Logic demonstrate improved translation accuracy, robustness to distribution shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention, establishing a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces in safety-critical applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Translating natural language instructions into machine-interpretable formal specifications enables robots and autonomous systems to plan, reason, and formally verify their behavior. However, existing translation models typically generate a specification for every input, even when the result is unreliable or fails to capture the user's intent, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Inspired by selective conformal prediction, we propose a selective translation framework that not only generates formal specifications but also determines when they can be trusted. Reliability is scored by two complementary black-box signals, the fidelity of the specification back-translated into natural language and the dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence, which fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone. Conformal risk control calibrates this score into a decision that accepts a specification or abstains, with a distribution-free bound on the rate at which incorrect specifications are accepted for execution, and a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs before any translation is attempted. The proposed framework is general across formal specification languages, with experiments on Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL) demonstrating improved translation reliability, robustness under the evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-quality long-horizon training data for terminal agents is expensive to produce, often costing hundreds to thousands of dollars per task, because each task must keep the instruction, environment, reference solution, and verifier mutually consistent. Human authoring does not scale, and direct generation with large language models (LLMs) often breaks these dependencies. We present Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST), a recursive verified synthesis framework for constructing long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at scale. Starting from verified seed tasks, RST extends the reference solution, realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, validates the result in a fresh sandbox, and reuses accepted tasks as seeds for subsequent rounds. Across fifteen recursive rounds, RST produces 37,484 synthesized terminal-agent tasks at roughly \$0.05 per task. Task difficulty increases substantially over rounds: the median reference solution grows from 67 to 374 lines, the median number of executed commands grows from 40 to 244, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90\% at $R_1$ to 2.5\% at $R_{15}$. To demonstrate training utility, we collect rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories on the synthesized tasks and use them for supervised fine-tuning. Fine-tuning on these trajectories improves Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B by up to 10 points on Terminal-Bench~2, Terminal-Bench Hard, and Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, while agentic PPO lifts Qwen3.5-27B to 49.44\%, 32.00\%, and 22.07\% on the three benchmarks, corresponding to relative gains of 20.0\%, 41.2\%, and 21.9\% over the base model. Moreover, after 15 rounds, the recursion shows no ceiling: synthesis yield and validation rates remain stable as difficulty keeps climbing, indicating that the process can continue well beyond the scale reported here.

items.title: Researchers analyze reliability and limits of innovation-residual auditing for autonomous data analysis agents, focusing on error localization, false flag control, and identifiability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Innovation-Residual Auditing of Autonomous Analysis Agents: Localization, Detection Limits, Error Control, and Identifiability
items.summary:
This paper examines the reliability of innovation-residual auditing methods used to identify errors in autonomous data analysis agents that perform tasks like cohort selection and model fitting with minimal supervision. The study evaluates how different scoring approaches affect the ability to localize errors, the spread of error flags across operations, and procedures to control false positives without requiring a correct model fit. It also establishes fundamental limits on error detectability, showing that small errors may be indistinguishable from normal variation among sound analyses, with representation size posing a greater constraint than training data volume.

The authors quantify how error detection varies depending on whether scores compare operations to immediate predecessors or longer reconstructions, and provide guidelines for choosing comparison lengths when errors accumulate gradually. They also analyze how audit guarantees weaken when models are imperfect or when analyses are selected for review based on their content. The findings highlight challenges in attributing minor errors and suggest that increasing the amount of sound training data yields diminishing improvements in detection limits due to representation dimensionality constraints.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents now carry out entire data analyses, selecting cohorts, joining tables, and fitting models with little step-by-step supervision. When such an analysis turns out to be wrong, someone must determine which operation caused it. A recent approach does this without any labelled mistakes, learning instead from analyses known to be sound and flagging operations that depart from what that model predicts; how reliable such audits are has not been studied. This paper supplies that analysis. The choice of score determines whether an error can be localized at all. If each operation is scored by how surprising it is given the operation immediately preceding it, then operations that merely inherit an earlier error are indistinguishable from correct ones, so one mistake produces one flag; scores computed against a longer reconstruction of the intended analysis instead spread a single mistake across many operations. We quantify how far they spread, and how to choose the comparison length when an error accumulates gradually rather than at once. We then give procedures that control the proportion of falsely flagged operations within a single audited analysis, requiring only that sound analyses be exchangeable rather than that the fitted model be correct, and we quantify how much the guarantees weaken when the model is imperfect or when the analysis was selected for review in a way that depends on its content. Finally we establish a limit on what any such audit can report: errors below a certain magnitude cannot be attributed at all, being indistinguishable from ordinary variation among sound analyses. This limit falls so slowly as more sound analyses are collected that at the representation sizes now in use a hundredfold increase reduces it by under two percent, so the dimension of the representation rather than the volume of training data is the binding constraint.

items.title: Researchers introduce CAP framework to measure and detect preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy in 17 large language models across 12 advice domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Measuring and Detecting Harmful AI Sycophancy
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Contrastive Anchor Probing (CAP), a framework to collect labeled data and detect preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS) in large language models (LLMs), where models reverse initial stances to align with user preferences. They applied CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, gathering 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday advice domains, revealing PSRS rates ranging from 5% to 56%, with more capable models showing less sycophancy.

The study demonstrates that PSRS can be detected from response text alone, though detection performance declines on unseen models, highlighting challenges in cross-model generalization. The researchers propose initial solutions to this issue and plan to release their dataset and code to support further research in identifying harmful sycophantic behavior in AI systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sycophantic responses are becoming pervasive in large language models (LLMs), and prior work has pointed out that some of them could be harmful. This paper focuses on one harmful sycophancy: preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS), where a model reverses an initial stance merely to align with a user's stated preference. While existing research mainly measures how sycophantic a model is, we go further and ask whether PSRS can also be detected automatically from a single response. To investigate this at scale, we introduce CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a framework for collecting labeled PSRS data. Applying CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, we collect 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. We organize our study around three research questions. (1) How often does PSRS occur? (2) How well can it be detected? (3) How does detection generalize to unseen models? We first reveal that PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Next, we show that detecting PSRS is feasible from the response text alone, and detectors need to learn subtle PSRS patterns from the training data. Because new LLMs appear rapidly, detectors inevitably encounter unseen models, making cross-model generalization an important framework goal. We demonstrate that detection performance drops on unseen models and propose an initial approach to address this challenge. We will release our dataset and code to support future research.

items.title: Researchers propose verifier-free test-time self-correction method for LLM reasoning that refines multiple reasoning rollouts through iterative critique and majority voting, improving accuracy on math benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers introduce a breadth-depth refinement framework for large language model (LLM) reasoning that uses test-time compute to explore and improve candidate solutions without relying on external verifiers. The method samples multiple independent reasoning rollouts, iteratively self-critiques and self-corrects each, and aggregates refined answers by majority voting, balancing diversity and error correction. Evaluated on benchmarks including AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500, the approach consistently outperforms greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based selection, beam search, and lookahead decoding across several open-weight models, with notable accuracy gains such as increasing Qwen2.5-1.5B's MATH500 accuracy from 58.0% to 32.5% on AMC. These results suggest that refining sampled trajectories at test time can be more effective than simply increasing sample size or relying on verifier models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning by using additional inference compute, but wider sampling alone can suffer from diminishing returns: new rollouts often repeat existing answer patterns instead of adding useful reasoning diversity. Verifier-based selection offers an alternative, but its performance depends on the calibration of an external reward model. We propose a verifier-free breadth--depth refinement framework that uses test-time compute to both explore and improve candidate solutions. The method samples multiple independent reasoning rollouts, refines each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction, and aggregates the refined answers by majority voting. Breadth preserves diverse initial attempts, while depth repairs local reasoning errors before aggregation. Across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500, our method consistently improves over greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-$N$, beam search, and lookahead decoding across multiple open-weight models. For instance, with Qwen2.5-1.5B, accuracy increases from the strongest verifier-based baseline to $58.0\%$ on MATH500, and from $25.0\%$ to $32.5\%$ on AMC. These results show that test-time compute can be more effective when used to refine sampled trajectories rather than only to sample more candidates or rely on verifier-guided selection.

items.title: Researchers propose INTraJ, a two-stage trajectory prediction framework separating planning and reaction, achieving state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Unified Framework for Trajectory Prediction with Explicit Planning and Reaction Decomposition
items.summary:
Researchers introduce INTraJ, a unified framework for trajectory prediction that explicitly decomposes social influence into a planning stage, which anticipates others' future behaviors to construct reference trajectories, and a reaction stage, which adjusts locally based on residuals. This approach supports both multi-target and single-target prediction paradigms and demonstrates improved performance, particularly in final displacement error and long-horizon consistency, across four standard benchmarks including Argoverse 2 and ETH/UCY.

The study highlights that social interactions in trajectory prediction function in staged roles, with planning preceding reaction, and validates that this decomposition leads to more stable and accurate predictions. The INTraJ code has been made publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trajectory prediction has shifted toward structured formulations with explicit social modeling. However, existing methods inadequately distinguish the functional roles of social influence in trajectory planning. Observing that agents typically form motion plans by anticipating others' future behaviors before making local reactive adjustments, we identify social interactions as playing staged roles, namely planning precedes reaction. We propose INTraJ, a unified framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: a planning stage constructs reference trajectories using future social information, and a reaction stage recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. INTraJ supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks, including Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD, demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in FDE and long-horizon consistency, with state-of-the-art performance achieved in several settings. INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling is critical for stable predictions. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/11isnotavailable/INTraJ.

items.originalTitle: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
items.summary:
DreamGuard is a new runtime guardrail designed for large language model (LLM) agents that interact with external tools and real-world systems, aiming to prevent unsafe actions that could cause irreversible harm. Unlike existing reactive guardrails that assess only immediate action safety, DreamGuard uses a risk-aware world model to maintain a latent state over the agent's trajectory and predict future risks, enabling proactive intervention decisions before actions are executed.

The system was evaluated across four benchmarks and an online guardrail test, outperforming reactive and other proactive baselines by achieving the best balance between safety and utility. DreamGuard also maintains low latency, averaging 25 milliseconds per call, making it efficient for real-time applications involving LLM agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents increasingly invoke external tools and interact with real-world systems, unsafe actions may cause irreversible consequences on external states, user data, and downstream services. Recent runtime guardrails mitigate such risks by checking proposed actions before execution, but many remain reactive: they primarily assess the apparent safety of the current action, lacking an explicit model of how risk evolves across the trajectory. This limitation creates a critical blind spot for long-horizon risks, where individually benign-looking actions can gradually drift the agent toward hazardous states. In response, we propose DreamGuard, a proactive guardrail for LLM agents built around a risk-aware world model. The world model maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the trajectory and predicts future latent states from which DreamGuard derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence. It then fuses these multi-horizon signals into intervention decisions before execution. Experiments across four benchmarks and an online guardrail evaluation show that DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines, achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among evaluated guardrails, and maintains an average end-to-end latency of 25 ms per call.

items.title: Researchers introduce Unified Agent, a stateful AI system managing interactions across devices and time with improved state design and performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Unified Agent: Managing Interactions across Devices
items.summary: Researchers propose Unified Agent, an AI system designed to manage user interactions across multiple devices and moments by maintaining a compact, action-ready state that organizes engagement evidence and requests. This approach addresses limitations in existing single-agent and multi-agent systems that struggle with scattered observations and state management across devices and time. The team developed a benchmark to compare state designs and found that Unified Agent significantly outperforms adaptations of four published designs. The system's advantage remains robust across different multimodal large language model families, capabilities, and reasoning efforts. The researchers plan to make their code and data publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.05729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As capabilities rapidly increase, AI agents can move from running inside one app to acting across a user's devices over time. Yet existing agent systems still fall short in this scenario. This is because observations are scattered across devices and moments, but mainstream systems are not designed around this fact: a single agent that treats devices as tools lacks effective state management for all devices across time, and multi-agent systems coordinate across agents but do not maintain the compact carried state a cross-device, cross-time request needs. We argue that the agent should maintain an effectively designed state that organizes engagement evidence, stated facts, and the standing request in a compact, action-ready form for deciding its action given the current observation. To compare state designs, we construct a benchmark of user-agent interaction across devices and time. We instantiate this principle in Unified Agent, a stateful agent that carries interaction evidence across devices and moments and uses it with the current observation to act. In the default setting, it significantly outperforms our adaptations of four published designs. Across changes in multimodal large language model (MLLM) family, capability, and reasoning effort, it remains ahead of all compared systems, demonstrating that the state-design advantage is robust across MLLM settings. Our code and data will be publicly available on GitHub.

items.title: Researchers identify irreversible skill contamination in self-evolving LLM agents and propose Verifier-as-Gatekeeper to pre-commit filter harmful skills, improving performance and transferability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When Self-Evolution Backfires: Pre-Commit Gating against Skill Contamination in LLM Agents
items.summary: Researchers found that self-evolving large language model (LLM) agents accumulate skills from their execution trajectories, but beyond a critical pool size, adding new skills can degrade performance due to irreversible contamination chains formed by defective skills. They propose Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG), a system that filters skills before admission using three critics—structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, and semantic consistency—combined with subset selection to prevent combinatorial contamination. On the Terminal-Bench 2 benchmark, VaG improved performance consistently, achieving 72% pass@1 with a skill pool five times smaller than unfiltered accumulation, and its skill pool transferred effectively to other models and benchmarks without re-evolution. Ablation studies confirmed that each critic intercepts distinct harmful skills, highlighting the necessity of pre-commit gating to maintain and improve LLM agent capabilities.
